records.title: Function calling with the Gemini API
records.relevance_note: Current provider doc with explicit multi-call, mode, and parser-handling semantics.
records.reason_included: Directly affects harness parsing, state threading, and response ordering.

claim_snippets.claim_text: Gemini 3 generates a unique id for every function call; manual histories and REST callers should return the matching id in functionResponse.

Function calling modes include AUTO, ANY, NONE, and VALIDATED; ANY forces function calls and guarantees schema adherence, while VALIDATED permits either natural language or function calls with schema adherence.
Parallel function calling supports multiple independent calls, and tool responses must be sent back in the same order requested.
The Python SDK can automatically execute functions by converting Python callables to declarations, detecting function calls, running them, and sending the responses back.

When combining built-in tools and function calling, functionCall, toolCall, and toolResponse parts may coexist in one turn, so callers should iterate all parts rather than assume functionCall is in a fixed position.

records.title: Gemini 3 Developer Guide
records.relevance_note: Gemini 3 Developer Guide is a official doc source with details on thought signatures, strict turn validation relevant to tooling tool gateway.
records.reason_included: Included for source-local evidence on tool gateway, state, execution loop.

claim_snippets.claim_text: Gemini 3 uses thought signatures to maintain reasoning context across API calls, and strict function calling validates the current turn; missing signatures cause a 400 error.
For parallel function calls, only the first functionCall part contains the signature and the parts must be returned in the exact order received.
For multi-step sequential tool use within one turn, every accumulated thought signature must be preserved in history.
In streaming, a thought signature may arrive in a final chunk with empty text, so stream parsers must check empty-text chunks for signatures.

records.title: HyFunc: Accelerating LLM-based Function Calls for Agentic AI through Hybrid-Model Cascade and Dynamic Templating
records.relevance_note: Direct methodology paper on accelerating function-call generation for agents.
records.reason_included: Provides mechanism and latency tradeoff details for large tool surfaces.

claim_snippets.claim_text: HyFunc identifies three major redundancies in function calling: processing large function libraries on every request, using a large model to generate a mostly predictable sequence, and generating boilerplate syntax token by token.
Its hybrid-model cascade uses a large model to distill user intent into a single soft token, then uses that signal for lightweight function retrieval and a smaller prefix-tuned generator.
Dynamic templating injects boilerplate parameter syntax on the fly inside an extended vLLM engine instead of having the model generate all structural tokens.
On unseen BFCL tasks, HyFunc reports 0.828s latency with 80.1% performance, outperforming baselines at comparable scale.

records.title: XGrammar-2: Efficient Dynamic Structured Generation Engine for Agentic LLMs
records.relevance_note: Structured-generation paper targeting dynamic tool-calling and response protocols.
records.reason_included: High-value source for grammar-enforced invocation and runtime overhead control.

claim_snippets.claim_text: XGrammar-2 targets dynamic structured generation workloads such as tool calling and response protocols where structure can vary across and within requests.
It introduces TagDispatch for dynamic structure switching and Cross-Grammar Cache for substructure-level reuse across grammars.
The engine combines an Earley-based adaptive token mask cache, JIT compilation, and repetition state compression to reduce dynamic-grammar overhead.
Experiments report more than 6x faster grammar compilation than prior structured-generation engines with near-zero end-to-end overhead.

claim_locations.locator: Abstract, opening sentences on dynamic structured generation tasks.

records.title: SimpleTool: Efficient Function Calling via Independent Argument and Tool Name Decoding
records.relevance_note: Direct tool-calling methodology paper on independent decoding of tool names and arguments.
records.reason_included: Covers latency, parallel decoding, and how to handle parallel-call benchmarks.

claim_snippets.claim_text: SimpleTool introduces special tokens that compress low-entropy function-call tokens by about 4x to 6x and act as mode selectors for independent decoding of function name and arguments.
It reports 3x to 6x end-to-end speedups, up to 9.6x, with only 8.2% overhead from the parallelization machinery.
With quantization, a Qwen3-4B model reaches 61.2 ms P50 latency and 16 Hz control on consumer hardware.

For benchmarks with parallel tool invocations, the method decomposes them into sequential single-step samples using history-based decomposition and random shuffling of prefix calls to teach order independence.

records.title: Function calling | OpenAI API
records.exception_reason: Canonical pre-window provider documentation for JSON-schema function tools, free-form custom tools, CFG-constrained invocation, and parallel-call caveats.
records.relevance_note: Foundational provider doc for multiple invocation modes and grammar constraints.
records.reason_included: Still one of the clearest primary sources on grammar-enforced and free-form tool invocation.

claim_snippets.claim_text: OpenAI distinguishes function tools defined by JSON Schema from custom tools that accept free-form text inputs and outputs.
For large function sets or large schemas, the guide recommends pairing function calling with tool search so only relevant tools are provided at runtime.
Parallel function calling can be disabled with parallel_tool_calls=false; built-in tools do not support parallel calls; strict mode may be disabled for some fine-tuned multi-call settings.
Custom tools can constrain free-form inputs using context-free grammars expressed in lark or regex formats.

Complex grammars may be rejected or yield syntactically valid but semantically wrong outputs, and the guide recommends simplifying grammars, reducing overlapping terminals, and tightening tool descriptions.

records.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
records.exception_reason: Foundational canonical source for inline reasoning-plus-action traces, the standard reference point for ReAct-style text-emitted tool invocation.
records.relevance_note: Canonical source for text-emitted ReAct-style invocation methodology.
records.reason_included: Necessary foundational anchor for inline action traces as a tool-calling method.

claim_snippets.claim_text: ReAct interleaves reasoning traces with task-specific actions rather than separating planning from acting.
Reasoning traces help the model induce, track, and update action plans and handle exceptions, while actions gather external information from APIs or environments.

On HotpotQA and FEVER, ReAct reduces hallucination and error propagation by interacting with a simple Wikipedia API; on ALFWorld and WebShop it reports absolute success gains of 34% and 10% over imitation and reinforcement learning baselines.
